title: Online Keno in Canada: Odds, Payouts and Reality
excerpt: Online keno looks simple and pays big, but the maths is unlike any other casino game. A clear look at keno odds, house edge and how Canadians should play it.
author: Lisa Davids
bodyHtml:
Online keno occupies a strange position in the Canadian casino lobby. It is one of the easiest games to understand — pick numbers, watch twenty get drawn, get paid for matches — and one of the hardest to evaluate, because the same game can carry a house edge of four per cent or twenty-five per cent depending entirely on which paytable you happen to be sitting at. No other casino game varies that wildly under a single name. If you play online keno without checking the paytable, you are not playing a known game; you are playing an unknown one that happens to share a name with it.

How the game works

A keno round uses a pool of 80 numbers. You choose a group of them — your 'spots', typically anywhere from one to ten, sometimes up to fifteen or twenty. The game then draws 20 numbers at random from the 80. You are paid according to how many of your chosen numbers appear among the 20 drawn, using the paytable attached to the number of spots you picked.

That is the entire game. There are no decisions after the numbers are locked in, no strategy that changes the draw, and no sequence of outcomes that affects the next round. Every draw is independent. This makes keno the purest form of a fixed-odds casino game and also the one where the paytable is the only thing that matters.

The maths, in plain terms

Your chance of matching numbers is fixed by combinatorics and is identical at every casino in the world. Pick 10 spots, and the probability of catching all 10 is roughly one in 8.9 million. Catching 9 of 10 is around one in 163,000. Catching 5 of 10 — which most paytables treat as a modest win or a push — happens about 5 per cent of the time. Those numbers cannot be changed by the operator.

What the operator sets is the payout for each of those outcomes, and that is where the house edge comes from. Two casinos can offer identical 10-spot keno with wildly different returns, because one pays 1,800x for a 9-catch and another pays 1,200x. The odds are the same; the price is not.

The practical consequence is that the return to player figure on keno spans a huge range. Well-designed online keno from a reputable studio typically returns somewhere in the low 90s per cent. State and provincial lottery keno, and poorly designed casino versions, can return in the 70s. That is a gap of twenty percentage points on the same game — enormous compared with, say, the difference between two blackjack tables.

How many spots should you pick?

There is no universally optimal number, but there are clear trade-offs, and the paytable decides the answer for any particular game.

  • Few spots (1-4): frequent small wins, low volatility, modest top prizes. Your bankroll lasts longer and swings are gentle. On many paytables these are also the better-priced bets in house-edge terms.
  • Middle spots (5-8): the compromise most players settle on. Realistic chances of a meaningful hit within a session, with top prizes large enough to be interesting.
  • Many spots (9-15): lottery-style. The advertised top prizes are spectacular and the probability of reaching them is negligible. Long stretches of nothing are the normal experience, not bad luck.

The important thing is that picking more numbers does not improve your expected return. It only redistributes the same expected return into rarer, larger payouts. A player choosing 10 spots is not being more aggressive in a way that pays off over time — they are choosing a higher-variance version of the same losing proposition.

Reading a keno paytable before you play

This is the entire skill of the game, and it takes ninety seconds. Open the game's info panel and check:

  • The stated RTP. Reputable providers publish it. If a keno game does not disclose a return figure anywhere, that absence is itself the answer.
  • The payout for near-maximum catches. The 9-of-10 and 8-of-9 style outcomes are where paytables differ most and where most of a good game's value sits.
  • Whether low catches return anything. Some paytables pay a small amount for 0 catches on high-spot tickets, which materially affects the experience if not the maths.
  • Multi-race or multiplier options. These usually alter the effective return, sometimes favourably and sometimes not. Check rather than assume.

Keno versus the rest of the casino lobby

Compared with the games around it, keno is expensive entertainment. A well-played blackjack hand costs well under one per cent of a bet in expected loss. A good online slot returns around 96 per cent. Even a mediocre keno game rarely matches that, and a bad one is among the worst-value products in a legal casino.

That does not make it a bad choice for everyone. Keno is slow, calm, cheap per round, and completely decision-free, which is exactly what some players want from a session. The mistake is playing it under the impression that it is comparable value to the games beside it. If your priority is stretching a bankroll, the return figures in our guide to online blackjack and video poker will do considerably more work for you, and online bingo offers a closer match in pace and mood with a social element keno lacks.

If you do want to play keno, the version matters more than anything else. Provider quality and paytable transparency vary enormously between operators, which is why our Canadian casino reviews look at game libraries rather than just bonuses, and the most searched casino games in Canada guide gives a sense of where keno sits relative to what Canadians actually play.

Keno strategy claims worth ignoring

Because the game is old and simple, it attracts an unusual amount of nonsense. Hot and cold numbers, 'due' numbers, patterns on the grid, and systems for choosing consecutive numbers all have exactly zero effect on outcome. Each draw is independent and uniform. A number drawn in the last five rounds is precisely as likely to appear in the next one as any other.

The only real decisions in online keno are which game to play, which paytable to accept, how many spots to choose given your tolerance for variance, and how much to stake per round. Everything else is decoration. Set a budget for the session before you start, treat the game as the slow-paced entertainment product it is, and do not let a large advertised top prize persuade you to play a paytable you would otherwise have walked past.
